extraction.title: Potential and Pitfalls of Audio as Data for Political Research: Alignment, Features, and Classification Models
extraction.venue: Political Analysis 34: 312-328 (published online 30 January 2026; open access)
extraction.document_type: Journal article (methods paper with applications; replication code on Harvard Dataverse doi:10.7910/DVN/K3I16E and GitHub)
extraction.coverage: Full text read: all 853 lines of C:\Users\pgoff\Documents\research\_text\ca7a80494661.txt, including the abstract, Sections 1-5, Tables 1-3, Figures 1-4 captions and content, footnotes, and the reference list. Metadata hint confirmed (title, 2026, Political Analysis 34: 312-328, DOI); the hint's "Mestre, Ryan" is corrected to two authors, Rafael Mestre and Matt Ryan (University of Southampton). Paul's own markup: no markup files were listed for this item, so paul_markup is empty.
extraction.research_question: Can audio be made usable as data for political research, given the "alignment crisis" (large text and audio corpora that do not intersect at the utterance level), and which audio features (LLDs, MFCCs, learned embeddings) and classifiers are useful for speech characterization, speaker identification, and emotion/valence measurement? The paper is a methods-and-applications demonstration; it does not test a substantive hypothesis.
extraction.theory: No formal theory is tested. The framing draws on the text-as-data literature (Grimmer and Stewart 2013; Wilkerson and Casas 2017) and on the claim that nonverbal audio cues (pitch, energy, intonation) carry political meaning not captured by transcripts (Section 2; Klofstad 2016; Dietrich et al. 2019; Damann, Knox and Lucas 2025). Emotion is treated as socially and politically constructed (Section 4.4, p.325), so classifier outputs are framed as starting points, not measures of emotion.
extraction.data: Unit: utterance/sentence within televised U.S. presidential and vice-presidential debates. Period: 1960 to 2020 (first televised debate 1960; 2020 included). Videos: 45 (243,023 s = 4,050 min = 67.5 h). Transcripts: 47,150 sentences (38,649 from candidates; 8,501 from moderators, panelists, or audience), originally from the USElecDeb60To16 dataset (Haddadan, Cabrio and Villata 2020), taken from the Commission on Presidential Debates site and extended to 2020, with some sentence omissions fixed (Section 4, p.317). Participants: 34 candidates (16 Democrat, 15 Republican, 3 independent), 82 moderators/panelists, 59 audience members. Video source: Commission on Presidential Debates YouTube channel. Note for the record: the speaker-identification section (Section 4.3, p.321) reports 44,559 sentences and 156 speakers, which does not reconcile with the 47,150 sentence count in Section 1 (p.314); the paper does not explain the gap. Forced-alignment validation used a random subset of 500 utterances, each rated five times by crowd annotators (p.318). Emotion models were applied to the debates; their training corpora were IEMOCAP (about 12 h of acted and improvised audio, Busso et al. 2008) and MSP-Podcast v1.7 (about 84 h, Lotfian and Busso 2019).
extraction.method: Four applications of increasing complexity (Section 4, Table 2). (1) Forced alignment: aeneas, which matches MFCCs of the audio to synthetic-voice MFCCs via dynamic time warping; validated by human ratings on a 1-5 scale. (2) Speech characterization: pYIN pitch (F0) in 32 ms rolling windows and RMS energy per utterance, normalized by each debate's average loudness; within-speaker pitch deviations averaged over 5 s windows (Figure 3c). (3) Speaker identification: a custom CNN on MFCCs (two blocks of convolution, max-pooling and dropout) versus a single-layer neural network on 768-dimensional wav2vec2-base embeddings (Hugging Face facebook/wav2vec2-base); Adam, learning rate 0.001, cross-entropy loss, batch 32 (MFCC) or 8 (wav2vec2), early stopping with patience 3 (footnote 9). (4) Emotion: off-the-shelf models, not retrained: a SpeechBrain wav2vec2 model fine-tuned on IEMOCAP for four classes (anger, happiness, sadness, neutral), and Wagner et al. (2023) dimensional models for arousal, dominance and valence trained on MSP-Podcast. Text-based emotion and sentiment classifiers are compared with audio-based labels as a cross-check (Figure 4d).
extraction.identification: None in the causal sense. This is a measurement and feasibility paper. Validation is by human crowd ratings for alignment (Section 4.1), held-out test accuracy for speaker identification (Table 3), and reported third-party benchmark accuracy/CCC for emotion models (Section 4.4). The paper explicitly says cross-speaker comparisons are confounded by microphone placement, compression, and sampling (p.320), and recommends within-speaker shifts or speaker-dependent human validation (p.324).
extraction.scope: Population: U.S. presidential and vice-presidential general-election debates, 1960-2020, all televised debate audio available on the CPD YouTube channel. Institution: candidate-moderator debate format, not legislatures. The paper argues the LLD and MFCC features are language-agnostic, but wav2vec2 embeddings and the emotion models are trained on specific languages and corpora and may not generalize across languages, accents, or cultures (Sections 3.3 and 5, pp.316, 326). Alignment and ASR context also draws on parliamentary data (UK Hansard/ParliamentTV, German Bundestag work) only in the literature review.

key_findings.finding: MFCC-based forced alignment of audio to transcripts performs well on crowd ratings; about 5% of text-audio pairs were rated not aligned at all, and short or interrupted sentences drove the poor alignment.
key_findings.numbers: 500 utterances, 5 annotations each; percentage agreement (PA) 85.26%; distance-based agreement (DA) 95.76%; about 5% rated 1 (not aligned at all).

key_findings.finding: Pitch extraction ranks candidates by average F0. Women candidates (Palin, Harris, Clinton) appear among the top five; the bottom five include Reagan, Lieberman, Edwards, Cheney and Dole. Pitch-based comparisons are presented as exploratory and confounded by recording conditions.
key_findings.numbers: 34 candidates; top five by average pitch include three of the four women candidates in the sample (Ferraro ranked sixth).

key_findings.finding: Normalized energy differs most across the two debates involving women candidates. Palin and Ferraro had lower average energy than their opponents (Biden, H.W. Bush).
key_findings.numbers: Energy normalized by each debate's average loudness; largest energy gaps appear in the Palin-Biden and Ferraro-Bush debates (no effect size reported).

key_findings.finding: Within-speaker pitch variation is far higher in 2020 than in the 1960 Kennedy-Nixon debate, which the authors link to changing norms and technology but do not test.
key_findings.numbers: Comparison of 1960 and 2020 first debates, normalized to each speaker's own baseline, averaged over 5-s windows; no statistic reported.

key_findings.finding: Wav2vec2 embeddings substantially outperform MFCCs for speaker identification, and the gap widens as the number of speaker classes grows.
key_findings.numbers: Individual debates: MFCC 0.888 (+/-0.085) vs wav2vec2 0.974 (+/-0.024). All 156 speakers: MFCC 0.081 vs wav2vec2 0.914 (table 0.08103 vs 0.913568). Candidates only, 34 labels: MFCC 0.134 vs wav2vec2 0.946.

key_findings.finding: Off-the-shelf emotion models label a large share of utterances as angry, with most of the rest neutral; sad and happy are rare. The authors say the four-label scheme is too simple.
key_findings.numbers: Reported IEMOCAP four-class test accuracy of 75.3%; no per-debate figures given in text beyond the plotted percentages.

key_findings.finding: Candidates with higher pitch (Clinton, Kemp) also score as more angry, and low-pitch candidates (Cheney, Lieberman) score as calmer. The paper says these contradict expert coding of Trump, who is not among the top angry candidates in the model output.
key_findings.location: Section 4.4, p.323, Figure 4b; contradiction cites Bucy et al. 2020
key_findings.numbers: Bucy et al. (2020) expert coding of the 2016 Trump-Clinton debate: Trump anger/threatening tone 82.6% of interventions vs Clinton 35.3%.

key_findings.finding: Dominance-arousal profiles place Clinton, Perot and Anderson at high dominance and high arousal; Lieberman and Cheney are lowest on both. No candidate stands out on valence.
key_findings.numbers: Model CCC for arousal 0.744, dominance 0.655, valence 0.638 (reported for the Wagner et al. 2023 model on MSP-Podcast, p.323).

key_findings.finding: Audio-based emotion labels and text-based labels only partly agree. Text emotion models mostly output neutral, while the audio model is more differentiated. Anger co-occurs with negative sentiment in 32% of cases.
key_findings.numbers: Anger-negative sentiment co-occurrence 32% (as reported in text).

limitations: Forced alignment is poor for very short or interrupted sentences (Figure 2b; p.318).

Cross-speaker and cross-time comparisons of pitch and energy are confounded by microphone placement, audio compression, sampling, and recording technology (pp.319-320, 324). The paper explicitly warns against naive interpretation.
Emotion and valence outputs are not validated against human coding of these debates; the authors call for speaker-dependent human validation (p.324).
Emotion classifiers can encode and amplify gender, ethnicity and vocal bias, possibly labeling women as angry when using neutral or assertive tones (pp.324-325).
Four-label emotion categories are simplistic (p.324). Emotion definitions vary across individuals, circumstances and cultures (p.322).
Training corpora (IEMOCAP, MSP-Podcast) are not debates; out-of-domain generalization is assumed from reported benchmarks, not tested here (p.322).
Embeddings are language-specific and computationally expensive for typical researchers; MFCC/LLD features are language-agnostic but less accurate for complex tasks (pp.316, 326).
Only U.S. presidential and VP debates are studied; the authors note the need for comparative work outside the U.S. (p.322).
Copyright prevents sharing the videos; broadcasters gave contradictory answers on rights, and CBS quoted a licensing fee from $2,500 (footnote 4, p.314).
Data-protection and copyright concerns apply when audio is sent to external ASR APIs such as Google or YouTube (p.314, footnote 2).
Sentence count does not reconcile between Section 1 (47,150) and Section 4.3 (44,559); the paper does not explain the difference (pp.314, 321).
Reported ASR error rates (WER 0.03-0.26) come from prior lab-condition validations that do not account for noise or crosstalk (Proksch, Wratil and Wackerle 2019; p.314).
measures: Word error rate (WER) and match error rate (MER) (background, footnotes 1 and 3; cited figures from prior work)
Percentage agreement (PA) and distance-based agreement (DA) for alignment ratings (Supplementary Appendix D)
Pitch F0 via pYIN, 32 ms rolling windows (p.319)
Root-mean-squared energy, normalized by debate average loudness (p.319)
Classification test accuracy for speaker identification (Table 3)
Discrete emotion label percentages (angry, happy, neutral, sad) per debate and per candidate (Figure 4a-b)
Dominance, arousal and valence scores; concordance correlation coefficient (CCC) for model benchmarks (pp.322-323)
Co-occurrence matrices between audio emotion and text emotion/sentiment labels (Figure 4d)

summary_md:
Mestre and Ryan (Political Analysis 2026) is a methods paper on audio as data. Its corpus is 45 U.S. presidential and VP debate videos (1960-2020; 47,150 transcript sentences). It runs four demonstrations. (1) Aeneas MFCC/DTW forced alignment, rated by crowd workers on 500 utterances x 5 ratings: percentage agreement 85.26%, distance agreement 95.76%, and about 5% of pairs not aligned at all, mostly short or interrupted sentences. (2) pYIN pitch and RMS energy. Energy is normalized by each debate's loudness, and within-speaker pitch deviation is shown over time. (3) Closed-set speaker identification. A single layer on mean-pooled wav2vec2-base embeddings reaches 0.914 accuracy across 156 speakers; a CNN on MFCCs reaches 0.081. (4) Off-the-shelf emotion models. The authors say these are biased by gender and pitch, and they disagree with expert coding.

For Melange the paper is less outside evidence than a method source. The speaker-identity research layer already copies it closely: `b5_audio_neural_head.py` reproduces the wav2vec2/Adam/batch-8/patience-3 head and cites section 4.3 and footnote 9, and `b5_audio_align_turns.py` uses Aeneas as the paper does. Melange's run of that same method on congressional audio failed. The fresh-21 neural EER was .226, against a bar of 5% or less. That run split train and test by source and event and used weak caption labels. The paper's 0.914 is in-domain debate audio, where the authors themselves warn that microphone placement and compression confound comparisons across speakers. So the paper's accuracy is not a benchmark Melange should expect to reach. The paper also backs the within-speaker pitch design and the fix for the sex confound in pitch variability. It cautions against the cross-member pooled eGeMAPS z-scores, which have no per-recording loudness or channel control. Its warnings about emotion models support keeping audio display-only.

bearings.paper_claim: Speaker ID: one neural layer on 768-d mean-pooled facebook/wav2vec2-base embeddings, Adam lr 0.001, cross-entropy, batch 8, early-stopping patience 3. It beats an MFCC CNN. Forced alignment uses aeneas (MFCC vs synthetic-voice MFCC, matched by DTW).
bearings.paper_location: Section 4.3, p.321, Table 3, footnote 9; Section 4.1, p.318
bearings.system_side: The research identity layer implements this head 'paper-exact' with no hyperparameter search, and it cites the paper by section. Embeddings are paper-faithful wav2vec2-base, with ECAPA as a separately labelled engineering comparator. Aeneas MFCC/DTW boundaries are the preferred alignment path, with a local Whisper ASR word_match cross-check. All of it is .candidate, with 0 production consumers.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The method transfers as a recipe. The brain note (single-look cases 2-3) already marks which parts are paper methods (embeddings over MFCC, forced alignment over ASR) and which are Melange adaptations (ECAPA, the EER at or below 5% bar, Whisper as cross-check). Paul's position table lists 'No annotated literature' for this component, but the code cites this paper.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-audio-speech#Acoustic speaker-ID (closed) and two-check identity design (proposed)|Acoustic speaker-ID (closed) and two-check identity design (proposed)]]

bearings.paper_claim: wav2vec2 reaches held-out accuracy of 0.914 across all 156 speakers, 0.946 across 34 candidates, and 0.974 (+/-0.024) within single debates, against MFCC at 0.081, 0.134 and 0.888. The authors warn that cross-speaker acoustic comparisons are confounded by microphone placement, compression and sampling.
bearings.system_side: Melange ran the same wav2vec2 single-layer method on a fresh cohort of 21 members. It used 3 train sources, 1 early-stopping source, 1 calibration source and 1 untouched test source, with caption hard-signal labels. Calibration EER was .226 against the 5% bar, so the status is FAILED_WEAK_LABEL_SMOKE. Earlier cosine (11/30) and linear-head (EER .317) attempts also failed.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's task is closed-set identification inside one broadcast series. It does not describe event- or source-disjoint splits, so speaker and channel are entangled, which is the confound the authors flag themselves. Melange's task is verification across independent programs, with weak labels and mixed venues (C-SPAN floor, studio, remote, phone). The paper's 0.914 therefore sets no expected level for congressional audio. The gap is consistent with channel leakage in the paper's setting, but that explanation is UNVERIFIED (DE-062): no second path has tested it.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-audio-speech#Acoustic speaker-ID (closed) and two-check identity design (proposed)|Acoustic speaker-ID (closed) and two-check identity design (proposed)]]

bearings.paper_claim: Aeneas alignment, validated by humans on 500 utterances x 5 ratings: PA 85.26%, DA 95.76%. About 5% of pairs were rated 1 (not aligned). Poor alignment is concentrated in very short or interrupted sentences.
bearings.system_side: Turn windows are trusted only when turn word_match >= 0.80 and hearing word_match >= 0.70. Clips need >= 50 target words and >= 30 s. Any Aeneas structural mismatch fails the whole hearing closed. Per the brain audio-pipeline note, the 0.80/0.70 bars are asserted and were never calibrated against human gold.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper supports a word floor that drops short turns and supports preferring forced alignment. It cannot calibrate the 0.80/0.70 bars, because its metric is human 1-5 ratings, not ASR word_match. Debate transcripts (CPD, moderated turns) are also cleaner than hearings, where crosstalk and govinfo text edits can be expected to lower alignment. The paper's 500 x 5 crowd-rating protocol is a ready template for the missing human calibration.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-audio-speech#Acoustic speaker-ID (closed) and two-check identity design (proposed)|Acoustic speaker-ID (closed) and two-check identity design (proposed)]]

bearings.paper_claim: Pitch-level comparisons across speakers mostly reflect speaker and voice. Women candidates fill three of the top five places by average F0 (34 candidates). The authors therefore recommend within-speaker shifts measured against each speaker's own baseline (Figure 3c, 5-s windows) or speaker-dependent human validation.
bearings.system_side: topic_emotional_intensity is a within-speaker F0 deviation: semitones are converted to Hz and standardized against the member's own baseline, with at least 5 speech units and 2 topics. pitch_variability_raw was found sex-confounded (r(F) = -.266 over 1,324 clips / 309 members; r(F, F0 mean) +.551). Commit 4193f0140 changed it to plain semitone SD.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The direction carries over from debates to congressional speech because F0 sex differences are physiological and do not depend on venue. The paper reports no effect size for the gender pattern, so the system's own r values remain the operative numbers. The paper validates nothing about trait meaning, so the audio-as-Big-5 route stays closed.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-audio-speech#eGeMAPS prosody and Whisper disfluency rates|eGeMAPS prosody and Whisper disfluency rates]]

bearings.paper_claim: Energy is only compared after normalizing by each debate's average loudness. Even then, pitch and energy differences across speakers and eras are confounded by microphone placement, compression, sampling and recording technology, and the authors warn against naive interpretation.
bearings.system_side: The member cache is built from duration-weighted means of raw eGeMAPS functionals per member. These are z-scored across all members pooled together (mean/SD over members, clipped at +/-5), with no per-recording loudness or channel normalization in the code. The brain note records channel (studio, remote, telephone) as uncontrolled, and a venue ladder for disfluency (live WJ about 26 per 1k words, NPR 0.22 per 1k).
bearings.transfer_conditions: This applies to every cross-member reading of volume_dynamics, pitch level or strain, including the descriptive layers that feed Fable narratives. Within-member and reliability (ICC) uses are less exposed. The paper's per-recording normalization is a cheap mitigation that Melange has not adopted. Pause and pace may be less channel-sensitive than loudness, but the paper does not test that.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-audio-speech#eGeMAPS prosody and Whisper disfluency rates|eGeMAPS prosody and Whisper disfluency rates]]

gaps_exposed: Melange has no human-rated alignment validation. The paper shows a cheap protocol: 500 utterances x 5 crowd ratings, reported as PA/DA. Melange's ALIGN_MIN_TURN_WORD_MATCH 0.80 and ALIGN_MIN_HEARING_WORD_MATCH 0.70 (fec/audio_rules.py:38-39) are still uncalibrated assertions, and the 150-clip annotation packet was never coded.

The member eGeMAPS cache (fec/members/b5_audio_build.py:85-100) has no per-recording loudness or channel normalization. The paper normalizes energy by each debate's average loudness before any cross-speaker comparison.

The cause of the transfer failure is undiagnosed. The paper's wav2vec2 recipe gave 0.914 on in-domain debates and EER .226 on Melange's event-disjoint split. No experiment yet separates channel leakage from weak labels or venue mismatch. Training and testing within one venue/channel would separate them, but that would be a new look and needs Paul's go.

Melange has no audio emotion layer. If one is ever proposed, the paper's evidence requires speaker-dependent human validation and a check for gender and pitch bias first. High-pitch candidates scored as more angry, and the model disagreed with Bucy et al.'s expert coding (Trump anger in 82.6% of interventions vs Clinton 35.3%).
flags: Do not quote the paper's 0.914 (156 speakers) or 0.946 (34 candidates) wav2vec2 accuracy as what Melange should expect. The paper measures closed-set identification within one broadcast series; Melange measures event-disjoint verification. On Melange's own fresh-21 cohort the same recipe failed at EER .226.

Paul's position table lists 'No annotated literature' for melange-audio-speech.identity-two-check-design. The code (b5_audio_neural_head.py:4, b5_audio_neural_pilot.py:225) and the brain single-look cases 2-3 note both cite Mestre & Ryan 2026 as the method source, so the table is stale.

The paper's internal counts do not reconcile: Section 1 gives 47,150 sentences, and the speaker-ID section gives 44,559 sentences and 156 speakers. Name the denominator whenever the speaker-ID figures are quoted.
The idea that channel leakage explains the gap between the paper's accuracy and Melange's EER is agent analysis and is UNVERIFIED (DE-062).
No conflict with D-021, D-025 or the rejected SNA proposals. The paper has no network, lobbying or influence content.
paul_alignment: The paper mostly agrees with where the system has landed. On prosody, Paul is interested in non-textual channels, and the paper agrees that pitch and energy carry political signal. It also says cross-speaker readings are confounded by recording conditions and that emotion outputs are 'starting points, not definitive measures'. That supports the system's ruling that audio is display-only and that audio-as-Big-5 is closed, and it argues against a stronger use than Paul's interest might suggest. On speaker verification, Paul asked for a framework for 'contextual or auditory constraints'. This paper partly answers that request, and the system has already adopted its alignment and embedding methods. Paul's per-component notes are stale here: they record no literature for the identity design, while the code implements this paper's head almost exactly. The notes also do not record that the method failed to transfer to congressional audio (EER .226).

related.why: Both papers use the within-speaker pitch-deviation design. Mestre & Ryan cite Dietrich, Hayes and O'Brien for it, and Melange's topic_emotional_intensity code names Dietrich explicitly (b5_audio_descriptors_candidate.py:209-210). Dietrich applies it to House floor speech.
A companion 'X as data' methods paper for images and video. It raises the same validation and bias cautions for non-text political channels.
A speaker-personalized prosody model. It matches the paper's advice to prefer speaker-dependent over cross-speaker acoustic readings, and Melange already used it in the sex-confound test.
Asks whether voice features carry trait information, which is the inference Mestre & Ryan warn against for emotion. Read together they bound what Melange's prosody descriptors can claim.

extraction.title: Corpus-Based Dictionaries for Sentiment Analysis of Specialized Vocabularies
authors: Douglas R. Rice (Dept. of Political Science, University of Massachusetts Amherst)
Christopher Zorn (Dept. of Political Science, Pennsylvania State University)
extraction.venue: Not named in the text. Title page dated July 20, 2018, and the text says materials will be posted to the Political Science Research and Methods Dataverse. The file name says PSRM R&R, so the venue is the PSRM revise-and-resubmit draft, unconfirmed by the text itself. Metadata hint is consistent with this.
extraction.document_type: Journal manuscript, revise-and-resubmit draft (dated July 20, 2018). Not a published article.
extraction.coverage: Full text read: all joined text lines of the PDF (33 pages in manifest; text pp.1-32 plus references). Figure 1-5 glyph matrices (text-extraction noise) were skipped; their captions and in-figure accuracy labels were read. Appendix is referenced (footnotes 9, 15) but not included in the file. Nothing in the paper touches lobbying, networks, path-finding, allocation, elections, persuasion/turnout, or legislators as subjects; the only human units are Supreme Court justices (as authors of majority opinions) and movie reviews. paul_markup: no annotation file exists for sha 3f615e2017a1 in _annots, and the manifest lists n_annots = 0, so there are no highlights, underlines, or sticky notes to report.
extraction.research_question: Can a "minimally-supervised" sentiment dictionary built from the corpus itself (seed words plus GloVe word-vector similarity) yield valid sentiment measures for specialized vocabularies where standard dictionaries (LIWC, AFINN) fail? The paper then applies the method to U.S. Supreme Court majority opinions to measure tone across 1792-2010, including over time and per justice.
extraction.theory: Distributional hypothesis: words used in similar contexts have similar meanings (p.4-5). Word vectors trained on a domain corpus place sentiment-laden words near seed words, so a small seed set grows a domain-appropriate dictionary. Standard dictionaries embed fixed valences that may be wrong in specialized contexts (e.g., "love" and "bagel" in tennis, p.3-4). Semantic drift over time is handled by re-estimating dictionaries on temporal subsets (p.19-20). The paper argues sentiment in court opinions is a substantive proxy for justices' disagreement and the norm of consensus (p.17-18).
extraction.data: Movie reviews (benchmark): Large Movie Review Dataset, 100,000 IMDB reviews (25,000 positive, 25,000 negative, 50,000 unlabeled). Word vectors were trained on 75,000 documents (12,500 positive, 12,500 negative, 50,000 unlabeled); 25,000 held-out test documents were used for an out-of-sample check (p.9-11). Mean review length 184 tokens, max 2,085 (p.13). Supreme Court: all cases 1792-2010 from justia.com, split into opinion-level files; only majority opinions retained; matched to the Supreme Court Database (Spaeth et al. 2012). About 26,000 unique majority opinions spanning 217 years (p.18-19). Mean majority opinion length 2,097 tokens. Justice-level analyses cover justices with more than 50 majority opinions; the text cites 84 justices (p.23). Unit of analysis: document (review or majority opinion), aggregated to justice-level means.
extraction.method: Minimally-supervised dictionary construction. (1) Train GloVe word vectors (text2vec in R) on the corpus: 300 dimensions, Xmax = 10, context window 50 tokens, drop the 20 most frequent tokens, tokens in more than 90% of documents, and tokens appearing fewer than 90 times, with AdaGrad (p.6-9). (2) Seeds: 10 uncontroversial positive terms (e.g., "superb", "brilliant", "great") and 10 negative terms (e.g., "bad", "awful", "horrible") (fn.3, p.7). (3) Extract the top 500 positive and top 500 negative words by cosine similarity to the seed-sum vectors, removing SMART stop words and AFINN opposite-valence terms (fn.4, p.7-9). (4) Weight token counts by tf-idf and by cosine similarity to get similarity-weighted positive and negative counts (Wp, Wn). (5) Polarity = (sum Wp - sum Wn) / (sum Wp + sum Wn), centered and scaled for comparison (fn.6, p.8). Accuracy uses a zero cutpoint. Sensitivity tests: corpus size (Figure 2), number of extracted words (appendix), and temporal re-estimation. Validity: benchmark accuracy against assigned ratings (with comparison to LIWC, AFINN, and supervised baselines in Table 1), convergent validity (polarity vs. number of dissenting votes, Figure 3), and discriminant validity (justice-level differences from LIWC and AFINN, Figures 4-5).
extraction.identification: None in the causal sense. The paper is a measurement-validity paper. Validity is assessed by (a) classification accuracy against the benchmark review ratings, in-sample and on a held-out 25,000-review set; (b) convergent validity with voting divisions (number of dissenting votes); and (c) discriminant validity against LIWC and AFINN justice-level estimates and against historical narratives. The Supreme Court validity evidence is described as "suggestive - though not conclusive" (p.25).
extraction.scope: Population: English-language movie reviews from IMDB (benchmark), and all U.S. Supreme Court majority opinions available from justia.com for 1792-2010 (about 26,000 opinions). Institution: the U.S. Supreme Court. Era: 1792-2010, split into pre-1891 (Evarts Act), 1891-1925 (Judges Act and the start of the consensus norm's decline), and post-1925 windows (p.19-20). Claims are limited to document-level polarity. The paper says the method is not a universal substitute for supervised learning (p.15).

key_findings.finding: Corpus-based dictionary polarity classifies movie reviews more accurately than standard dictionaries. In-sample accuracy is 80.4% (12,004 negative, 12,663 positive, 332 neutral) versus 69.4% for LIWC (with scaling) and 71.3% for AFINN.
key_findings.numbers: 80.4% vs 69.4% (LIWC) vs 71.3% (AFINN); 12,004 neg / 12,663 pos / 332 neutral

key_findings.finding: Out-of-sample (held-out 25,000 reviews) accuracy is consistent with in-sample accuracy: 79.5% for the corpus-based approach, 69.7% for LIWC, and 70.6% for AFINN.
key_findings.numbers: 79.5% (ours, held-out) vs 69.7% (LIWC) vs 70.6% (AFINN)

key_findings.finding: Accuracy gains hold across corpus sizes. Even 5,000-document corpora beat the LIWC and AFINN accuracy figures, and accuracy approaches standard machine-learning levels by about 15,000 documents. Accuracy rises with corpus size, with diminishing returns after about 30,000.
key_findings.numbers: 5,000 docs beats 69.4%/71.3%; ~15,000 docs reaches roughly 80%; mean review 184 tokens (max 2,085)

key_findings.finding: Compared with supervised classifiers on the same movie-review benchmark, the approach matches Naive Bayes, MaxEnt, and SVM (about 79-80%) but falls short of Pang and Lee (2004, 87.15%) and Maas et al. (2011, 88.05%). The paper stresses it uses no classification labels.
key_findings.numbers: Ours 80.4; Pang, Lee and Vaithyanathan (2002) NB 79.7, MaxEnt 79.7, SVM 79.4 (mean); Pang and Lee 2004 87.15; Maas et al. 2011 88.05

key_findings.finding: Dictionaries estimated on temporal subsets of the Court's opinions differ sharply. Only 34.0% of negative and 27.7% of positive terms carry over from the early Court to the turn-of-century Court; only 24.2% of negative and 19.6% of positive terms carry over from the turn-of-century Court to the modern Court.
key_findings.numbers: 34.0% neg / 27.7% pos (early to turn-of-century); 24.2% neg / 19.6% pos (turn-of-century to modern)

key_findings.finding: Convergent validity: only the corpus-based polarity measure declines consistently as the number of dissenting votes rises. LIWC and AFINN show increases in polarity at various points, most notably in 6-3 decisions. In the modern era, the corpus-based measure treats unanimous opinions as generally positive.
key_findings.numbers: Qualitative pattern across dissent counts; no coefficient reported

key_findings.finding: Discriminant validity: the corpus-based justice-level polarity is only moderately correlated with LIWC and AFINN. The Spearman rank correlation between LIWC and AFINN is 0.64, but the corpus-based measure correlates 0.29 with LIWC and 0.16 with AFINN. The standard deviation of justice-level mean polarity is 0.25 (ours), 0.22 (LIWC), and 0.16 (AFINN).
key_findings.numbers: rho(LIWC,AFINN)=0.64; rho(ours,LIWC)=0.29; rho(ours,AFINN)=0.16; SD 0.25 / 0.22 / 0.16

key_findings.finding: Divergence between the corpus-based measure and LIWC/AFINN shows an inflection at 1925. The paper treats this as the point after which the measures diverge less.
key_findings.numbers: Inflection around 1925 (no coefficient reported)

key_findings.finding: Justice-level examples: Harold Burton ranks as the most positive justice in the corpus-based measure, while AFINN ranks him 14th of 84 and LIWC 50th. The corpus-based measure gives Chief Justice White a substantial drop in polarity. Chief Justice Waite is marginally negative in the corpus-based measure, versus marginally positive in LIWC. Chief Justice Taney wrote significantly more negative majority opinions than under either comparison dictionary. Historical narratives are cited as support, but the paper calls the evidence suggestive rather than conclusive.
key_findings.numbers: Burton: 1st (ours) vs 14th of 84 (AFINN) and 50th (LIWC)

key_findings.finding: Sample scale: about 26,000 majority opinions across 217 years, averaging 2,097 tokens per opinion, which the paper calls longer than the longest movie review.
key_findings.numbers: ~26,000 opinions; 217 years; mean 2,097 tokens

limitations: Not a substitute for supervised learning when labeled benchmarks exist; the paper says it does not argue for universal replacement (p.15).
Measurement is at the document level. It obscures which subjects receive sentiment, and it does not capture sentiment within documents, which matters for long opinions (p.27).
Generalizability to other specialized vocabularies is untested. The paper asks whether the method 'travels well' and flags within-document variation in sentiment-laden word use as a concern (p.27).
Dictionaries may include noisy non-subjective terms; the authors plan to adopt Pang and Lee (2004) subjectivity filtering in future work (p.27).

The Supreme Court validation relies on voting divisions, which the authors call an imperfect proxy because consensual norms mask disagreement, and on historical narratives; the paper calls the result 'suggestive - though not conclusive' (p.17, p.20, p.25).
Temporal splits (pre-1891, 1891-1925, post-1925) are chosen on theoretical grounds; the authors note rolling windows as an alternative for semantic-change studies (fn.14, p.19).
Accuracy is computed with a zero cutpoint, and neutral reviews (332) are excluded from accuracy; LIWC is reported with and without scaling (p.10).
Unlabeled reviews are retained in the word-vector corpus, which the authors describe as a conservative test (p.9, p.14).
Majority opinions only are analyzed; concurrences and dissents are dropped for comparability across eras (p.18).
Terms were not stemmed (fn.13, p.19).
The appendix (corpus-size and seed-set robustness, opinion-length density) is referenced but not in the PDF.
references_of_note: Grimmer, Justin and Brandon Stewart. 2013. Text as Data. Political Analysis 21(3). Dictionary validity concerns that motivate the paper.
Quinn, Kevin et al. 2010. How to Analyze Political Attention With Minimal Assumptions and Costs. AJPS 54. Minimal-assumption text measurement precedent.
Pennington, Socher and Manning. 2014. GloVe: Global Vectors for Word Representation. EMNLP. Word-vector method used.
Mikolov, Sutskever, Chen, Corrado and Dean. 2013. Distributed Representation of Words and Phrases. NIPS. Word2vec precedent.
Maas et al. 2011. Learning Word Vectors for Sentiment Analysis. ACL. Supervised benchmark at 88.05% on the movie-review data.
Pang and Lee. 2004. A Sentimental Education. ACL. Subjectivity-based benchmark at 87.15%; proposed refinement.
Pang, Lee and Vaithyanathan. 2002. Thumbs up? EMNLP. Naive Bayes, MaxEnt, and SVM baselines at about 79-80%.
Tang et al. 2014 and 2016. Sentiment embeddings that rely on emoticon labels. Cited as a barrier for political science uses.
Pennebaker et al. 2001 and 2007 (LIWC); Nielsen 2011 (AFINN). Standard dictionaries used as comparisons.
Spaeth et al. 2012. The Supreme Court Database. Source for matching opinions to case information.
Walker, Epstein and Dixon 1988; Haynie 1992; Caldeira and Zorn 1998; Hendershot et al. 2013. Dissent and consensual-norm measurement; voting divisions as the convergent-validity benchmark.
Danelski 1960. Chief justice leadership and the consensus norm.
Black et al. 2011 and 2016; Bryan and Ringsmuth 2016. Emotional language in courts; prior dictionary-based applications.
Gerner et al. 1994. Cost of building custom dictionaries.
Uszkoreit, Xu and Li 2009. Origin of the 'minimally supervised' term.
Lobbying, networks, path-finding, elections, persuasion/turnout: none cited.

Our approach offers a fast and flexible method of addressing this semantic shift.
the rank-order correlation of our measure with LIWC is 0.29, and with AFINN is 0.16.

summary_md:
Rice and Zorn (2018, a PSRM revise-and-resubmit draft) argue that off-the-shelf sentiment dictionaries break on specialized vocabularies. Their alternative starts from 10 positive and 10 negative seed words, trains GloVe vectors on the domain corpus (300 dimensions, 50-token window, terms seen fewer than 90 times dropped), keeps the 500 nearest words on each side, weights counts by tf-idf and cosine similarity, and scores polarity as (Wp-Wn)/(Wp+Wn). On 50,000 IMDB reviews this reaches 80.4% in-sample and 79.5% held out, against about 69-71% for LIWC and AFINN. It needs roughly 5,000 or more documents before it beats them. On about 26,000 Supreme Court majority opinions (1792-2010), justice-level polarity ranks correlate only 0.29 with LIWC and 0.16 with AFINN, while those two correlate 0.64 with each other. The choice of dictionary therefore reorders the units. The paper calls its court validation suggestive, not conclusive, and notes that document-level polarity cannot say which subject the sentiment is about.

For Paul's system the sharpest point is Stage 5b. press_value = DEBATE stance sign x stock Lexicoder LSD2015 intensity. LSD lists "credit" as positive and "debt*", "charge*", "risk*", "oversight*" and "fraud*" as negative, and run_stage5.R scores every release with no masking of those domain terms. I ran a quick one-path check on 1,563 text-bearing releases (UNVERIFIED, per DE-062). It found the effect real but small: 4.5% of positive mass and 7.0% of negative mass come from those terms, the release-level intensity rank correlation is 0.953 with and without them, and the LSD net sign flips on 4.1% of releases. The legacy regex scorer cites Rice and Zorn for its polarity formula, but its lexicon is hand-weighted. Its corpus-expansion helper departs from the paper's parameters and was never run. The paper is a measurement template the press layer has not yet applied, not a reason to change rankings.

bearings.paper_claim: General-purpose dictionaries carry valences that are wrong in specialized vocabularies (tennis 'love'). On the benchmark, a corpus-derived dictionary reached 80.4% (in-sample) and 79.5% (held-out) vs LIWC 69.4% and AFINN 71.3% / 70.6%.
bearings.paper_location: Abstract p.1; pp.3-4; Section 3 p.10-12, Figure 1
bearings.system_side: Stage 5b runs the stock LSD2015 dictionary (1,709 positive, 2,858 negative entries) on full release bodies, with no domain stoplist. Intensity is |pos-neg|/words. LSD lists 'credit/credits/credited' as positive and 'debt*', 'charge*', 'risk*', 'oversight*' and 'fraud*' as negative, so phrases like 'credit union', 'interchange charges' and 'NCUA oversight' are scored as tone. The brain records LSD's only validation as a 3-case smoke test (pro +4 / negated 0 / neutral 0). Local check, one path, UNVERIFIED (DE-062), 1,563 text-bearing releases in cu_press_stance_tone.csv: 'credit' tokens are 4.5% of LSD positive mass; debt/charge/risk/oversight/fraud are 7.0% of negative mass; Spearman between intensity with and without these terms is 0.953; the LSD net sign flips on 4.1% of releases. Spearman for press_value with vs without 'credit' is 0.976 among releases with nonzero stance.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's evidence covers polarity classification (movie reviews) and court opinions, not intensity, and not congressional press releases. The mechanism (domain nouns read as sentiment) does carry over and was observed directly in the LSD entries. The local check shows the effect is small at the release level and leaves ranks nearly intact. It says nothing about whether LSD intensity tracks human-judged heat, and the paper does not test that either. Member-level aggregates were not checked.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-stance#Lexicoder LSD2015 tone intensity|Lexicoder LSD2015 tone intensity]]

bearings.paper_claim: Polarity = (sum Wp - sum Wn)/(sum Wp + sum Wn), where Wp and Wn are counts weighted by tf-idf and cosine similarity over 500+500 words extracted from GloVe vectors (300 dimensions, window 50, minimum count 90) trained on the domain corpus from 10+10 seeds. Gains over LIWC/AFINN appear from about 5,000 documents and level off around 15,000-30,000.
bearings.paper_location: Section 2 pp.6-9, fn.3-6; Section 3.1 pp.13-14, Figure 2
bearings.system_side: The legacy scorer computes polarity with the Rice & Zorn formula, but Wp and Wn come from a hand-curated TONE_LEXICON with fixed weights of 1/2/3, plus phrase and bill bonuses. They are not corpus-derived similarity weights. The opt-in expand_tone_lexicon() helper departs from the paper: rank 50 vs 300, window 5 vs 50, term_count_min 5 vs 90, one bipolar axis (mean pos - mean neg) instead of separate seed-sum vectors, top 200 vs 500 terms, and a 50-document floor vs the paper's ~5,000. No lexicon_candidates.csv exists, so the helper has never been run. The lexicon is labelled 'toward credit unions', which merges tone and stance. The scorer was superseded for stance on 2026-06-21 after over-flagging 21 of 32 neutral releases, and it survives only as a comparison column.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The formula transfers as written, but the paper's validity results apply only to corpus-derived, similarity-weighted dictionaries, which this code does not build. The paper also says document-level polarity hides which subject gets the sentiment (p.27). That limitation supports the system's 2026-06-21 decision not to read CU stance from tone. The CU-relevant set has 1,563 text-bearing releases, below the corpus size at which the paper shows gains.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-stance#Legacy CU press regex stance and graded tone scorer|Legacy CU press regex stance and graded tone scorer]]

bearings.paper_claim: Changing the dictionary reorders units. Justice-level Spearman correlations are 0.29 (corpus-based vs LIWC) and 0.16 (vs AFINN), compared with 0.64 between LIWC and AFINN. SD of justice means: 0.25 / 0.22 / 0.16.
bearings.system_side: press_value = final_sign x abs(lsd_net_norm) (or lsd_charge). It is rolled up per member and category as a decay-weighted mean, and the workbook press columns feed the Press pillar through signed-extrema normalization. The magnitude part of the pillar therefore depends on a single instrument, and no alternative dictionary or sign-only variant has been compared.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The divergence evidence comes from court opinions spanning 217 years, where semantic drift is large. Press releases from 2022 on are a narrow window, so instrument divergence would probably be smaller. Within-LSD masking of domain terms barely moved ranks (rho 0.976, UNVERIFIED). A between-dictionary swap has not been measured. Press carries 0.10 weight in the live blend, which limits how far any reordering reaches the rank.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-stance#press_value aggregate and human-label overlay|press_value aggregate and human-label overlay]]

bearings.paper_claim: LIWC trails a domain-built measure on benchmark accuracy (69.4% vs 80.4%), and its unit-level rankings diverge from the domain measure (Burton ranks 1st in the corpus measure vs 50th of 84 in LIWC).
bearings.system_side: The live affective N measure is the E-residualized, party-controlled sum of LLM affective facets. The LIWC base (i + negemo - posemo) was removed as a component because it 'dragged in false positives' (Jack Bergman moving from #1 to #412). It is kept only as a convergent anchor (r = +.24, gate G3). The component description, which still says z(LIWC) + z(LLM), is stale relative to the code.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper measures document sentiment in reviews and opinions, while the system measures a trait in interview transcripts. Only the general claim transfers: generic closed-vocabulary counts misfire outside their home register. The paper does not test personality or speech.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-psychometrics#Affective neuroticism slot and N genre-transfer tests|Affective neuroticism slot and N genre-transfer tests]]

gaps_exposed: No domain stoplist or masking before LSD scoring: 'credit union', 'interchange charges', 'NCUA oversight', 'debt' and 'risk' count as tone in every CU release (stage5_lsd.R:48-61).

LSD intensity on congressional press releases has never been validated against human-coded intensity; the only check was a 3-case smoke test. Rice & Zorn's three-part design (benchmark accuracy, convergent validity against a behavioural proxy, discriminant validity against alternative dictionaries) is a ready template.
No dictionary-sensitivity test for the Press pillar: LSD intensity vs a corpus-derived dictionary vs stance sign only, measured as Kendall tau on Press% and on the top 133.

expand_tone_lexicon() was never run, and the CU-relevant corpus (1,563 text-bearing releases) is below the ~5,000-document size where the paper shows gains. A viable corpus-based dictionary would need the full unfiltered press corpus as the unlabeled training set, as the paper does with its 50,000 unlabeled reviews.

Document-level tone cannot say which target the tone is about (paper p.27). The system already handles this by separating stance (DEBATE, two-hop), but press_value still multiplies a target-specific sign by a target-blind magnitude.
flags: Citation fidelity: cu_press_release_scraper.R:131-132 and 2799 cite Rice & Zorn for the legacy polarity, but the weights are hand-assigned 1/2/3, not corpus-derived cosine/tf-idf. The expand helper departs from the paper on window (5 vs 50), dimensions (50 vs 300), minimum count (5 vs 90), seed geometry and corpus floor. Describe it as 'R&Z polarity formula over a curated lexicon', not as a Rice & Zorn dictionary.

The LSD domain-term contamination figures (4.5% positive mass, 7.0% negative mass, intensity rho 0.953, sign flips on 4.1%, press_value rho 0.976) are new agent analysis from a single path and stay UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces them (DE-062). Each figure covers 1,563 text-bearing releases in cu_press_stance_tone.csv; member-level aggregates were not checked.
Component record drift: melange-psychometrics.affective-n describes the measure as z(LIWC) + z(LLM), but emit_affective_n.py:39-43 uses LIWC only as a convergent anchor.

The paper's court validity is 'suggestive - though not conclusive' (p.25), and its benchmark is movie reviews. Do not quote the 80.4% vs 69.4% gap as an expected gain for congressional press releases.
No conflict with the barred SNA proposals, D-021, D-025 or the reciprocity rulings: the paper does not touch networks, lobbying or money.
paul_alignment: Paul has not annotated this paper (n_annots = 0), and his position note for legacy-regex-scorer says Rice & Zorn is "on disk but unannotated". The closest takeaway he has recorded is his highlight of Merkley & Stecula using Lexicoder with custom dictionaries, which points the same way as Rice & Zorn: tailor the dictionary to the domain. The built system uses stock LSD2015 with no customization, so it lags both his highlight and this paper. The local check suggests the cost is small (UNVERIFIED). His press-pillar note, which treats press scored by sentiment as an observable persona, is consistent with the system's split of stance sign from tone magnitude. The paper's p.27 limitation (document-level sentiment cannot identify the target) supports that split. Nothing in his notes is stale against this paper, except that the scraper code cites Rice & Zorn more strongly than it implements them.

related.why: The legacy scorer cites both papers together (cu_press_release_scraper.R:122-136): Haselmayer & Jenny supplies the graded intensity bands and negation handling, Rice & Zorn the polarity formula. Both are dictionary-construction alternatives to stock lexicons.

Also builds a lexicon automatically for a specialized domain, here direction-aware. The system tested it and rejected it (3 good / 43 bad sign changes), which fits Rice & Zorn's warning that whole-document dictionary scores do not identify the target.
Uses Lexicoder with custom dictionaries; Paul highlighted it. Rice & Zorn give the methodological case for customizing a dictionary instead of using LSD as-is, which is what Stage 5b does.
Meta-analysis of LIWC-Big Five validity. Together with Rice & Zorn's LIWC benchmark shortfall, it bears on the system's demotion of LIWC to an anchor in affective N.
Rice & Zorn use LIWC (Pennebaker et al.) as a comparison dictionary; this is the LIWC lineage paper in the vault.
Offers an LLM-based alternative to minimally supervised dictionaries for political text, the path the system took for stance (DEBATE) and for affective N.

backlinks.why: Rice & Zorn argue that general sentiment lexicons misfire on specialised vocabularies. Zhang applies the general Affin lexicon to retail tweets with no domain check.
Rice and Zorn's domain dictionaries are the lexical baseline lineage behind the legacy scorer. Khan's TF-IDF ladder is the supervised-classical step above it in the same stack.
Corpus-specific dictionaries are the evidence-based answer to the review's dismissal of word-matching methods. They also bear on whether a general LSD2015 suits congressional text.

meta.title: Using step and path selection functions for estimating resistance to movement: pumas as a case study
meta.venue: Landscape Ecology (vol. 31, pp. 1319-1335; published online 2 Nov 2015). Special issue: Multi-scale habitat modeling.

extraction.title: Using step and path selection functions for estimating resistance to movement: pumas as a case study
extraction.venue: Landscape Ecology (vol. 31, pp. 1319-1335; published online 2 Nov 2015). Special issue: Multi-scale habitat modeling.
extraction.document_type: Journal research article (ecology / landscape connectivity, GPS movement data)
extraction.coverage: Full text read in chunks (text file lines 0-1469): abstract, introduction, methods, results, discussion, conclusions, acknowledgments and the full reference list. The text file contains no appendices (Appendices 1-7) and no figure images; figures are described only through their captions (Figs 1-7). Paul's markup: the task list was "(none)", so no annotation files were opened and paul_markup is empty. Topic coverage: lobbying, elections, persuasion/turnout, legislators, allocation, text measurement and political networks are absent from the paper. Network content is limited to landscape connectivity (circuit theory via CircuitScape, current density) and path/step movement models; "path" here means animal movement trajectories, not graph path-finding.
extraction.research_question: Can step selection functions (SSFs) and path selection functions (PathSFs) be extended to model habitat selection during movement at multiple spatial scales, and how sensitive are the regression coefficients and predicted resistance surfaces to (a) SSF vs PathSF, (b) scale, (c) paired vs unpaired prediction framework, and (d) GPS acquisition interval (5 min vs 60 min)?
extraction.theory: Resource selection functions (used vs available design; Johnson 1980 third-order selection; Manly et al. 2002). SSFs (Fortin et al. 2005) and PathSFs (Cushman et al. 2010) are conditional logistic models of movement selection; predicted relative probability exp(sum b_i x_i) is inverted to give resistance. The paper argues that movement-based selection can differ from resource-use (point) selection, citing Squires et al. 2013, Elliot et al. 2014 and Zeller et al. 2014. Scale of analysis is defined as the Pareto-kernel radius (ecological neighborhood), not data grain.
extraction.data: Ten pumas (Puma concolor), six female and four male, Santa Ana Mountains, southern California; Lotek 4400S GPS collars set to 5-min fixes, Oct 2011 to Mar 2014. Collar duration 9-71 days (median 29). Final dataset 75,716 fixes after removing 2D fixes with PDOP above 5 (individual range 1,650-18,464; median 7,147). Unit of analysis: used/available step (steps of 200 m or more, buffered 30 m) and used/available 24-h path (n = 315 paths, 12 start-hour subsets averaged). Land cover: CalVeg vector data at 1:24,000, rasterized to 30 m, aggregated from 25 types to nine classes (chaparral 45%, urban 19%, coastal scrub 14%, annual grassland 6%, coastal oak woodland 5%, agriculture 5%, riparian 3%, perennial grassland 2%, barren/open 1%). Pseudo data: the 5-min data subsampled to 60-min fixes. Study period 2011-2014; no sex-specific analysis (sexes pooled).
extraction.method: Multi-scale SSF and PathSF with Pareto-weighted kernels. 19 time intervals (5 min, 20 min, then every 20 min to 360 min); generalized Pareto fitted per interval with gpd.fit (gPdtest); kernel radius = min(97.5th percentile of displacement, maximum observed displacement), giving scales of 532 to 7,390 m. Available area for each step/path = mean land cover proportion across kernels placed along the step/path. Predictors = differences in land cover proportion between used and available (no intercept, response always 1). Simple single-variable conditional logistic models at each scale; multiple models using the weakest-effect class as reference; characteristic scale = scale with largest absolute coefficient in simple models; multi-scale model combines characteristic scales. Mixed-effects (random puma) conditional logistic models failed to converge, so glm was used. Model performance: 10-fold cross-validation (Johnson et al. 2006) with Lin's concordance correlation coefficient (CCC). AIC compared only within SSF and within PathSF (equal sample sizes). Resistance predicted in unpaired (pixel-only) and paired (pixel plus kernel context) frameworks; resistance = 1/probability, not rescaled. Acquisition-interval bias: 60-min pseudo steps and paths treated against 5-min truth; bias = mean absolute difference in coefficients per cover type, averaged per scale. Connectivity: CircuitScape current density between protected areas on either side of I-15 (Temecula corridor); top 20 current-flow pixels along I-15 compared across resistance models.
extraction.scope: Population: ten pumas with established home ranges in one fragmented, urbanizing region (Santa Ana Mountains, southern California). Dispersing animals were not sampled and the authors say results may differ for them. Era: GPS data 2011-2014. Land cover from CalVeg (USDA Forest Service 2007). Methods are presented as general for SSFs/PathSFs at any GPS interval; empirical claims apply only to pumas in this study area.
extraction.identification: No causal identification strategy. Inference rests on the within-animal case-control design (each used step/path is compared with its own available area, which is the standard conditional logistic set-up), plus two internal comparisons: (1) 5-min data as truth versus 60-min subsampled pseudo data for the same animals, to isolate the effect of acquisition interval; (2) paired versus unpaired prediction from the same fitted coefficients, to isolate the effect of prediction framework. Out-of-sample performance is assessed by 10-fold cross-validation with CCC. Cross-method comparisons of AIC are explicitly not made.
measures: Relative probability of movement exp(sum b_i x_i)
Resistance = inverse of predicted relative probability (not rescaled or truncated)
Conditional logistic regression coefficients per land cover class
Land cover proportion difference between used and Pareto-kernel available area
AIC (within SSF and within PathSF only)
Bias = mean absolute difference in coefficients (5-min vs 60-min), averaged over cover types per scale
Count of top-20 current-flow pixels along I-15 (road-crossing candidate locations)

key_findings.finding: Regression coefficients are highly sensitive to the scale of analysis. Annual grassland and agriculture change sign across scales. For PathSFs, urban coefficients range about -10 to -30 and chaparral about -4 to -15.
key_findings.numbers: PathSF urban -10 to -30; chaparral -4 to -15; 19 scales from 532 to 7,390 m

key_findings.finding: Pumas show multiple characteristic scales of response during movement, described as mostly bi-modal. Coarse scales characterize urban and agriculture; fine scales characterize the remaining cover types (annual grassland, barren, chaparral, coastal scrub, perennial grassland, and others).
key_findings.numbers: Scales 532 to 7,390 m; 19 time intervals from 5 min to 360 min

key_findings.finding: PathSFs generally produced larger-magnitude coefficients than SSFs. Characteristic scales also differed between the two methods for every cover type except chaparral, most for coastal oak woodland and riparian. Annual grassland was the exception to the larger-PathSF pattern.
key_findings.numbers: Differences in characteristic scale for all types except chaparral

key_findings.finding: Predictive performance (10-fold CCC) rose with scale and PathSFs outperformed SSFs at all scales except the finest (532 m PathSF was the weak case). Best SSF CCC 0.976 at 6,555 m; best PathSF CCC 0.992 at 7,390 m. The multi-scale model did not have the highest CCC but was close: 0.943 (SSF) and 0.982 (PathSF).
key_findings.location: Results, Model performance, Fig. 4 (p. 1326); Discussion p. 1331
key_findings.numbers: SSF best 0.976 (6,555 m); PathSF best 0.992 (7,390 m); multi-scale 0.943 SSF, 0.982 PathSF

key_findings.finding: Within each method, AIC decreased with increasing scale. The multi-scale model had the lowest AIC for SSFs; the 6,555 m model had the lowest AIC for PathSFs. AIC could not be compared between SSFs and PathSFs because sample sizes differed.
key_findings.location: Results, Model performance (pp. 1326-1328, Appendix 3 not in text)
key_findings.numbers: SSF lowest AIC = multi-scale; PathSF lowest AIC = 6,555 m

key_findings.finding: Acquisition interval bias: 60-min pseudo data produced a consistent 3-4-fold difference in regression coefficients relative to 5-min data. Bias was larger for PathSFs than SSFs. Some cover types changed sign. Annual grassland and barren were preferred in 5-min steps but avoided in 60-min pseudo steps. Coastal scrub, avoided in the true steps, appeared preferred in the pseudo steps.
key_findings.location: Results, Acquisition interval bias, Fig. 5 (p. 1328); Discussion (p. 1331)
key_findings.numbers: 3-4-fold consistent difference; 60-min vs 5-min

key_findings.finding: Paired-framework resistance surfaces are more heterogeneous, with a greater range and larger maximum values, than unpaired surfaces. Unpaired surfaces assign one resistance value per cover type regardless of context. In the paired surfaces, urban produces rings of high resistance on entry but low resistance inside.
key_findings.location: Results, Sensitivity of resistance surfaces, Fig. 6, Appendices 5-6 (pp. 1328-1330); Discussion p. 1331-1333
key_findings.numbers: Urban (19% of area) gives highest unpaired resistance; 91st-100th percentile identical across unpaired surfaces

key_findings.finding: Resistance values were higher for PathSFs than SSFs and increased with scale. The finest scale had the lowest resistance range, especially for SSFs. The authors attribute the scale trend to coefficients becoming more negative as scale increases.
key_findings.numbers: Finest scale lowest range; resistance increases with scale

key_findings.finding: Road-crossing candidate locations (top 20 current-flow pixels along I-15) differed between SSF and PathSF, among scales, and between prediction frameworks. Locations were more similar at the same scale across methods and frameworks than within the same method across scales, so scale is a major driver of connectivity differences. Pseudo-step (60-min) models biased crossing locations and missed middle-I-15 sites, and SSF models also flagged sites absent from true-path models.
key_findings.location: Results p. 1330 (Fig. 7, Appendix 7 not in text); Discussion p. 1331
key_findings.numbers: Top 20 pixels along I-15 per model

key_findings.finding: Authors recommend PathSF models over SSFs when a choice is available, and caution that resistance surfaces and corridors are sensitive to method, scale and GPS schedule.

limitations: Only ten pumas, with sexes pooled; mixed-effects models with individual as random effect failed to converge, so glm was used and individual heterogeneity was not modeled (p. 1325).
Only land cover predictors were used; slope, topographic ruggedness and roads, known to affect puma selection, were excluded to simplify the methods (p. 1332).
Study animals had established home ranges; the authors state results may not hold for dispersers, who may select habitat at finer scales (p. 1331-1332).
The inverse of predicted relative probability is assumed to equal resistance; the authors state no empirical evidence supports this (p. 1333).

Whether the paired framework is superior to the unpaired framework, or a hybrid, is unresolved; the paired surfaces may not capture absolute fitness costs, and the authors note concerns about rings of high resistance around urban areas (pp. 1328-1333).
Resistance surfaces were compared visually and by distributional summaries only; no method for whole-surface validation was provided beyond road-crossing locations (p. 1333).
Connectivity analysis is a single illustrative CircuitScape run in one corridor (Temecula / I-15) and was described as cursory (p. 1326).
Bias was assessed only at one alternative interval (60 min); the optimal acquisition interval for pumas was not determined, and a shorter-than-5-min interval may be better (p. 1332).
AIC cannot be compared between SSFs and PathSFs because sample sizes differ, limiting method-level model selection.
The scale of analysis is the Pareto-kernel radius, and the grain was held at 30 m; the effect of grain was not examined.
The 24-h path analysis averages over 12 start-time subsets rather than estimating a single model.
Brownian bridge alternatives were suggested but not tested (p. 1333).

short_quotes.quote: Regression coefficients were extremely sensitive to scale and pumas exhibited multiple scales of selection during movement.
Given our results, when there is a choice, we recommend PathSF models be used over SSF models.
a mismatch between GPS collar acquisition interval and species vagility may ultimately bias corridor conservation planning
